preamble.summary: LXX Zephaniah tracks MT closely. The book is not directly cited in the NT. Its most influential contribution to later theology is the Dies Irae tradition — the great 'Day of Wrath' imagery of 1:14–18 in its LXX form, which supplied the liturgical and poetic vocabulary for medieval eschatological hymnody.
preamble.notable_variants: The eschatological 'day of the LORD' vocabulary in its LXX form (hēmera kyriou) that becomes the standard NT eschatological phrase; the 'pure speech' of 3:9 that early Christian writers read as a reversal of Babel.
preamble.theological_legacy: The Latin Dies Irae sequence hymn (likely 13th century) draws vocabulary and imagery from Vulgate Zephaniah 1:14–18, which in turn renders the LXX. The NT's hēmera kyriou eschatology (1 Cor 1:8, 5:5; 1 Thess 5:2; 2 Pet 3:10) builds on the LXX prophetic word-field of which Zephaniah is a concentrated expression.

renderings.lxx_reading: ὅτι τότε μεταστρέψω ἐπὶ λαοὺς γλῶσσαν εἰς γενεὰν αὐτῆς
renderings.mt_rendering: I will change the speech of the peoples to a pure speech
renderings.lxx_rendering: For then I will change upon peoples a tongue for its generation
notes: The LXX of this verse is obscure — 'a tongue for its generation' doesn't quite match either the Hebrew or natural Greek. Several Greek manuscript traditions preserve variants trying to clarify the verse.

Early Christian exegetes read Zephaniah 3:9 as a prophecy of Pentecost: God will reverse Babel by purifying the languages of the peoples. Acts 2's Pentecost narrative — many languages, one Spirit, one unified understanding — draws implicitly on the Zephaniah 3:9 reversal-of-Babel motif.
The 'pure speech' / 'shoulder to shoulder serving' pair in MT Zephaniah makes this verse a favorite proof-text for Christian universalism and for eschatological linguistic reconciliation.
